A coding tool just became a $60 billion asset.

SpaceX acquired Cursor — the AI-native code editor — for $60B this week, and simultaneously announced a $75B IPO. That valuation puts a developer productivity tool on par with major aerospace and defense companies.

This is a signal worth sitting with. The companies shaping the next decade do not see AI coding tools as nice-to-have upgrades. They see them as core infrastructure — on the same strategic tier as compute, propulsion, and supply chain.

For business leaders, the takeaway is direct: software velocity is now the primary constraint on how fast any company can move. AI development tools are the biggest lever on that constraint. And the window to build or acquire that capability as a competitive advantage is narrowing fast.

The standalone AI tool era is giving way to platform consolidation. If your engineering teams rely on third-party AI coding tools without a strategic integration plan, your dependency risk just increased materially.
